utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, would you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case Number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I turn to the Prosecution for the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone. For the Prosecution, Mathias Neuner, and myself Tecla Henry-Benjamin, and Ana Vrlic, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Defence appearances please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Mr. Hadzihasanovic. Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Alexis Demirdjian, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Mulalic Nermin, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber would like to welcome all those present in the courtroom, the representatives of the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, the accused and all the other staff in this courtroom, not forgetting, of course, the interpreters. We're going to continue today with the testimony of the witness from yesterday, so I'm going to ask the usher to have the witness shown in, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, in line 13, page 1, I think the interpretation is wrong., it's Ms. Ana Vrlic, case manager, not Mr. Daryl Mundis. He's missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That would be troubling indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope you had a good evening. You're going to finish your testimony today. We're going to have the follow-up questions. And without further ado, I'm going to give the floor to the person who's going to ask you those questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: My name is Tecla Henry-Benjamin and I am one of the representatives of the Prosecution in this case. As the President of the Trial Chamber stated to you yesterday, I am going to ask you a few questions, and I must say to you that if at any time you appear confused, or you need to have the question repeated, or you need any assistance, please feel free and I'll oblige. Thank you. Doctor, in response to my learned colleague yesterday, you said that in your practice you treated both civilians and troops. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Tell me, Doctor, is this the same thing as saying that you are an army at -- or rather, at the time you were an army doctor as well as a private practitioner?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both civilian and military.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us for which army you worked for. Did you work for all the armies or did you work for a specific army?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Doctor, you gave us your name as Enes Ribic. But during that period when you were in Mehurici, were you known by any other name or were you called by any other name?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They always referred to me as Dr. Ribic, Dr. Ribic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Do you have an alias name by the name of Ribo, Dr. Ribo?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They're different surnames. There is a surname Ribo, people living in a village in that area next to Mehurici. So they have the same root. For those of you who don't understand our language. Of course the root is R-i-b, but R-i-b-o is one surname and R-i-b-i-c is another surname. So I was actually a refugee living in Mehurici. I was -- I didn't originate for [as interpreted] Mehurici. The original population there are called Ribe or Ribo. The genitive is Ribe in the plural, but the nominative is Ribo.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation, Doctor. Can you for the benefit of the Trial Chamber tell us: How close was your clinic to the Mehurici school?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About a hundred metres, 120 metres perhaps. I never measured the distance, but that would be at roughly 100 to 120, let's say, metres. From 1996, I haven't been there, which means eight years, so I've lost the sense of distance. But it's nearby.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: If I were to say to you that a witness who testified here would have put the distance at about 50 metres -- your clinic at about 50 metres away from the school, would that be correct as well?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think that would be correct. It's not 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, did you ever practice at all in the Mehurici sports hall? Did you go there to tend to patients at any time?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not myself personally. I didn't go to give assistance there. There was my younger colleague Menzel and the lady doctor. They were closely connected. I was the primarius, that is to say higher up in rank as a doctor, but if they couldn't solve a problem, they would come to me. Although, if I remember correctly, as it's a long time ago, I wasn't called in to intervene. I didn't have any need to, because the lady doctor working with the civilians who were put up there had her assistant, Menzel, who was a younger colleague of mine and saw to those matters. If the two of them weren't able to solve a problem, then I would be called in as the reserve doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: You may not have practiced as you indicated to us, but you did indicate to us that your clinic was pretty close by to the school. Would you be able to assist the Trial Chamber as to whether the International Red Cross was present at the school?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I don't think it was there, although they didn't show it to me. So I can't really say yes or no. I don't know that there weren't. I can't be categoric in saying they weren't. But they weren't introduced to me, so I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: For clarification for the Trial Chamber, a witness in this court indicated that there was a medical corps at the school. Would I be correct in saying that the clinic -- the doctors you previously spoke of, is that considered as a medical corps? Would that be what the witness was referring to in the school?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In wartime, the conditions we were facing at time, it was excellent, maximum medical assistance, because there were rare occasions where you had three doctors at the same time at their disposal. So this was the maximum amount of medical care that you could expect, given the wartime conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Doctor, in the course of your practice, did you ever have cause to attend to the sick at the Zenica hospital?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't not. But I did cooperate with the Zenica hospital, and I said yesterday that I asked them for some sanitary material and medicines from time to time and some equipment, too. I didn't need to because in the Zenica hospital there were 150 doctors, so I would have just interfered. But I did have contacts from time to time, especially with the director of the hospital and the orthopedics department. Because the patients who came from my area were put up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And you just answered my other question. I was about to ask you if in fact you have referred patients to the Zenica hospital, but I think you answered it all. Have you -- during your tenure in Mehurici, did you ever know of a building referred to as the blacksmith shop?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I heard of something like that. That's a part of the facilities belonging to the forestry administration, forestry department. Yes, yes. I think I can say that I did hear about the blacksmith shop.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And would you be able to tell us how close was the blacksmith shop, approximately, to your clinic?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know where the blacksmiths actually were, but part of the blacksmith shop was adjoining the clinic itself. You have to go behind the forestry administration building and then you would come across the blacksmith shop. Actually, it's not just adjacent to the clinic, some 30 metres away. I don't know why in peacetime it was used. They were sort of small garages. They were being used as garages. I don't know about the technology of forestry departments, I didn't know why they actually used them for that. But during the war I did happen to see from time to time through a window that was right up against the clinic. People, faces would appear from time to time, people I would note standing at the window, in that blacksmith shop.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did you treat any patients from that blacksmith shop?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They never asked for my assistance, so no, I didn't treat them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yesterday in response to my learned colleague, you testified - albeit differently to other witnesses - that the conditions at the Mehurici school were good, given the conditions. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I experienced the wartime Golgotha, I knew the kind of conditions that other people were subjected to, civilians in wartime conditions. I said that for wartime that was the optimum that you could expect, the best conditions that you could expect to offer people given the wartime conditions. So yes, I think that they were good conditions, absolutely. Given the war that was on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, you not having a clinic at the Mehurici school, I take it that -- however, from your previous answer that you were familiar with the compound of the Mehurici school and the conditions which led you to say what you just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Defence has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object to the question put in that way because the witness, regardless of saying he was in the clinic, he did testify that he entered the sports hall several times and did have contact with the civilians there. So the assumption that he was just there is not the proper assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: In light of the previous question and your response, would you be able to assist the Trial Chamber as to who, in your opinion, was in charge of the detainees at the Mehurici school?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The system was, generally speaking, to have a civilian protection staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned colleague mentioned the word "detainees" in the music school, whereas the witness spoke about people who had been accommodated there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I would like to say that they were absolutely not prisoners. It would be a crime to say they were prisoners, detainees. They were people that were being taken care of. Because a prison is something quite different.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, would you say that these people who were at the Mehurici school, would you say that they were there of their own free will, their own free choice?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in a way it was salvation for them, given the war situation and the conflict, because it prevented them from being in a conflict situation and running the risk of being wounded or killed. So I think only somebody who was not looking at it from the safety aspect would say it was not a good place to be. I left my house as a refugee, and in Bosnia we call it Muhadjir. So I really do know what a refugee is when somebody is taking care of me. It was very important for me to have somewhere to sleep, to lie down. All right; in prisons, yes. You had conditions of that kind, that is to say you were given a place to sleep and some food to eat. But in wartime, I don't think that the people -- actually, I don't think the people had ever experienced a war and you don't know what the war experience and conditions mean. It's something that upsets your comfort and the standards you have become accustomed so to. You have to bring it down to basics. So it's not the best possible conditions, but that's common knowledge. It's wartime, after all. I do claim -- I was in school where there were refugees in Travnik - there were Catholics and Muslims there, and Orthodox people too - put up in a school in Travnik, as I say. Whereas in Mehurici, the conditions were much better for these people there, for those civilians of ours from the neighbouring village of Maline. And if you were to compare those conditions - and I was in a position to compare them, because I was also in Zenica, for example - at that place, what's it called. They were called collection centres, yes. With refugees from Jajce, Donji Vakuf, Prijedor, et cetera. So I did have the opportunity of comparing the standard of living of the Jajce refugees in Travnik and Zenica, for example, with the comforts of these civilians that were being taken care of in Mehurici. And it would be a crime to say that those people had poor conditions or worse conditions than the other refugees that were being taken care of in those school buildings. Usually they were sports halls, of course, in those schools. Perhaps I am taking up too much time but I really would like to bring that home to you. It would be a crime to say that they had worse conditions, for example, than other refugees in other places, in other towns, for example, as I say, and let me repeat in Travnik and Zenica which are much larger centres and larger towns where there were several thousand. I can't, of course, give you the exact number in Mehurici, for example, in the sports school. There might have been 100 to 150 people. I can't give you an exact number. But I think that they were provided with satisfactory conditions and the basics, given the situation that prevailed, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection. I did not want to interrupt the witness. He gave an extensive answer in response to my colleague's question. But I do have an objection to the kinds of questions put by my learned colleague because the nature of the indictment is not the unlawful incarceration of civilians, just treatment. So I should ask the Trial Chamber not to allow the Prosecution to continue putting questions along those lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the indictment, reference is made to cruel treatment I believe, so ask questions that have to do with Count 3 of the indictment, which sets out quite precisely what it says in the preamble and indictment. But please go on, Madam Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Doctor, could you for the benefit of the Trial Chamber state for us the type of injuries or illnesses that you commonly treated, both civilians and troops during this period, the period of the conflict when you were in Mehurici. Can you give us an idea of the type of injuries and illnesses that you may have treated during that time?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the conflict of the HVO and the army, BH army, I catered to all the civilians, as I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say that I'm not receiving the interpretation anymore.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was saying, before the conflict between the BH army and the HVO, the health service and health protection of the population functioned quite normally, those belonging to the clinic. And I would like to see a Catholic patient who said he was not well received. I really would like to see an example of that, because there were Orthodox who were treated there, too. So they had equal conditions, I'd like to repeat.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Doctor, one second before we go on and on. My question was very specific. Could you state for the Trial Chamber the kinds of injuries or illnesses that you would have treated, either the civilians or the troops, during the period of the conflict when you were stationed in Mehurici. Just give us a breakdown of the types of injuries you saw.

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the type of injuries and diseases as they usually are. They were colds, flu, pneumonia. Only once we had an epidemic of stomach typhus but they were standard diseases. And I would see to the lighter wounds that can be dealt with in clinics, traumas from, entrance/exit wounds, from chance injuries that occurred. And yesterday I gave the example of a wounded pregnant lady, in an advanced stage of pregnancy. That sort of stands out. I remember the woman because I felt very sorry for her.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. But if I may elaborate a little bit. Would injuries such as broken bones, severe bruising -- were you faced with those kinds of injuries?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes of course in wartime you have things like that, too. There were fractures, broken bones, and I gave the example of the young woman. But there were other fractures, too. If you mean bruising from beatings, that didn't exist. I never saw any bruises as the effects of somebody having been beaten up by someone.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: None of your patients, so to speak, from the Mehurici school who may -- who you may have assisted the lady doctor with, none of your patients so to speak, as far as you can recall, ever came into the clinic with broken bones, bruises, as far as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And as to the blacksmith shop. Do you recall receiving patients from the blacksmith shop?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I don't know that anybody ever said, This man is from the blacksmith shop. I received everybody who was brought in, but I wouldn't know where they were from. Nobody would have said this one here is from the blacksmith shop. And as I said yesterday in answer to the lady's question, the Defence counsel's question, I said that if you are referring to any mistreatment or abuse in the blacksmith shop, I'm not deaf. I hear very well and I see very well. My eyesight is very good and I am a great fighter for man and man's right. And I would never have allowed in my presence or anywhere near me somebody to be beaten up, even if he was a criminal or anything like that. I would stand up and ask for the man's protection. So I never heard any moans or cries, moans -- moans, I would say -- I don't know how the English booth are going to interpret that, but groans and moans. I never ever heard that. So that is something that is completely fabricated, something that somebody has thought up. It's just 10 metres away and I would have heard that. You couldn't hide anything like that. And I had sufficient authority and strength and the power to go to a headquarters, for example, and tell them, Stop doing what you're doing if they were doing anything like that. But no, I never had occasion to see anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Now, there came a time as you said in response to my learned colleague that you saw the emergence of foreigners in the area and after a while, after a time, these group of people increased. Now, bearing in mind of the oath you had taken as a medical practitioner to safe life and limb, and of course not to differentiate from any ethnic background or anything, could you state for the Trial Chamber if at any time at all in your practice you had treated mujahedins, or the foreign fighters as they're referred to.

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I ever treated any of them, but I saw them in my clinic too. Yesterday I said that I did come across these people because they married local women, they brought their wives there, and because they couldn't use their own medical service, that's why they brought their wives to me. I did see them but I did not treat them. I saw them because they were accompanying their wives.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did you on any occasion have reason to ever refer foreign or foreigners as they were called, mujahedins, to the Zenica hospital? Or did you at any time arrange for any mujahedin or mujahedins to go to the Zenica hospital for injuries received?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that my previous answer excludes this possibility. Since I didn't see any wounded men, I didn't treat them, it wasn't necessary for me to refer such people to a hospital. It wasn't necessary for me to take care of such people.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Would you -- bearing in mind the fact that you had said that you hadn't treated them but you knew of them, had you ever been to their new surroundings? You indicated to us that they were in Mehurici first and then you knew for a fact that they had moved to Poljanice. Could you tell the Trial Chamber if you personally had ever visited the camp.

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never visited it, but I did pass by the camp. When I had some free time, I went hiking and I passed by their camp, too. So I've seen it, but I didn't enter the camp. It wasn't necessary, as I said. I never asked them for anything. I asked for medical assistance from Travnik. I asked humanitarian organisations for assistance. So I never entered their compound from a distance of 50 metres -- at a distance of about 50 metres, there's a road. You could see that they had a gate from that distance. They had a place where guards would stand, but I never entered the compound. I didn't try to enter it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: If you had to describe the situation that prevailed in Mehurici at the time of the conflict, if you had to use one word to describe the situation, how would you have described it?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd say silly, unnecessary, really something that I would condemn -- I would condemn the people who had provoked that situation, and we know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I say to you that the presence of the foreigners, the mujahedins, aggravated the situation in Mehurici and perhaps could be partly responsible for the deterioration that took place?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, I'm not a military strategist, I'm a doctor. I don't think that made the situation deteriorate. Until the HVO units and the HVO leadership started carrying out actions that affected the situation, everything was calm. No one touched us. The mujahedin didn't touch us, we didn't touch them, they didn't touch anyone else. They didn't interfere with anyone else. I think this was an unnecessary conflict. It was unnecessary in Bosnia and especially in Mehurici. I don't think they would have touched or interfered with anyone. But I am a doctor, after all; I can't provide you with an expert opinion. I can provide you with an opinion about medical matters, but not really about military matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Well, doctor, I'll tell you why I chose that line of questioning: because yesterday in response to my learned friend, in particular page 81, line 10, you stated, and I quote that: "The HVO was responsible for the deterioration." Now, I know that you were a doctor or I know that you are a doctor, but it seems to me that you were expressing your opinion on the cause for the conflict, hence the reason for the question that preceded. So I'll ask you this now. Could you explain to us why you said that the HVO was responsible for the deterioration.

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned a blockade. You can't leave a place under blockade. You can't go to get medical aid. So whose responsibility is that? I didn't see an army checkpoint limiting movement, restricting movement. I don't know, but I can't really say there were no such checkpoints. But on Ovnak there was an HVO checkpoint, and there was one in Guca Gora as well. Half the civilians didn't even think of trying to pass through and army members couldn't do this either. But it was obvious that someone was creating a disturbance. Why impose a blockade? We were allies. Then all of a sudden someone started doing something that wasn't normal. This behaviour was the arrogant behaviour of a minor military force. That's how I would describe it. I'm not a member of the military, but I could assess the force of the respective parties and a minor force started establishing order. So that's the main reason, the main factor that indicates that something was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I say to you that the Croats were in the minority in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And would you agree with me if I said that their forces were less in manpower than the ABiH? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe you haven't understood me correctly. I was talking about the Bila region. I think that even in peacetime the Muslim population was in the majority. They represented 80 to 90 per cent of the population. That's why I said that the balance of forces was very different. The army was huge, there were a lot of people who joined the defence, but I must say that it was well-known that the army didn't have any logistics support. They weren't as well armed as the HVO. The HVO was technically superior, I think. I don't know the details, but we know that the HVO logistics support functioned very well in the war, which wasn't the case for the army. The army really didn't have good logistics support, not in any sense. The troops were hungry and thirsty and they had to go barefoot. They didn't have any weapons. Nevertheless, it's the troops that count in a war. And that's why I mentioned the balance of forces and I said that as far as this balance of forces concerned, the army and was more powerful because they had more troops than the HVO, far more troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Now, on the 8th of June, 1993, you said to my learned friend that the fighting was not necessarily in Mehurici but around about Mehurici. Could you for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, could you state for us who at that time was doing the shooting.

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't say. As I said at the time there was shooting. As to who was doing the shooting, I couldn't say. I wasn't at the lines. I said this is something you should ask others about. But I know there was shooting and the shooting became more and more intense. On that day there was a large-scale clash and there were wounded. As to who was shooting, I don't know. I was at some distance. But you should be in that area, in that valley, to hear how the shooting echoed. So it was evident there was a conflict somewhere there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So then, Doctor, in light of what you have just said, would you agree with me, then, that it would have been a very unfair statement on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. your behalf to say that the HVO was fully responsible for the deterioration, especially since you yourself didn't know who was doing the shooting?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that it's crazy behaviour, unreasonable behaviour, to attack someone who is stronger. But that's what the command was like. I think someone pushed them. This was an unnecessary act. These policies were unnecessary, they were crazy, and these are the policies that governed the HVO unit. As a man I would say that it was completely unreasonable. And I can confidently say that I never saw any BH army members threatening anyone. I didn't see any blockades, I didn't see them preventing people from taking food to others, I didn't see them preventing medical aid from being delivered. So the leadership was unreasonable. What did they want to do? Perhaps they wanted to do what we are discussing now. But the army really wasn't responsible for the conflict in the Bila Valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And just one final question, Doctor. Is it your evidence that the ABiH didn't have any checkpoints in the area?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say for sure. I was never stopped. I didn't have any insignia on me. I was in civilian clothes. But I don't remember ever being stopped by an army checkpoint. I drove around in my own vehicle and I was controlled, that's true, but I don't remember any checkpoints, any army checkpoints. People couldn't tell whether I was a Catholic or a Muslim because I didn't have anything that would enable them to identify me. So I never was stopped. I can't remember that. Some time has passed, so I can't remember that. But I do remember being controlled by the HVO. But as I said yesterday, they treated me fairly. I couldn't say that that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. You have been a most gracious witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, this concludes the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Before I give the floor to the Defence for additional questions, with regard to the objection raised by the Defence about the legal status of the people in the Mehurici school, I'd like to remind the Defence of paragraph 28 in the indictment. If you have a look at paragraph 28 in the indictment. I'll read paragraph 28: "Mainly Bosnian, Croats but also Bosnian Serbs, were unlawfully imprisoned and detained in ABiH detention facilities. Imprisoned ... Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Serbs were ... beaten, subjected to physical and/or psychological abuse, intimidation and inhuman treatment, including being confined in overcrowded and unsanitary conditions, and suffered inhumane deprivations of basic necessities such as adequate food, water, and clothing. They were provided little or no medical attention." That's what it says in paragraph 28 of the indictment. And as far as cruel treatment is concerned, you can find it under paragraph 41 -- in fact, cruel treatment is under Count 4. And as far as Mehurici is concerned in the indictment under paragraph 42, reference is made to imprisonment and detention. And for Mehurici, it's from paragraph 42(C) and (D). Under (C) it says: "In the Mehurici elementary school, members of the ABiH 3rd Corps 306th Mountain Brigade kicked prisoners while detained. During interrogation, prisoners were beaten and threatened by members of the 306th Brigade. The general food, hygiene and living conditions were poor." And that goes for the blacksmith shop. Because it says also the food, hygiene and living conditions were poor there too. That's what it says in the indictment. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good day, Mr. President. Good day, Your Honour. Mr. President, the question raised by my colleague a little earlier on concerning legal attention mention the fact that there is no charge. The accused haven't been charged with the illegal detention of people or for having failed to prevent their illegal detention or for having failed to punish people who may have illegally imprisoned others. In paragraph 28 in the indictment we have an introduction, and in light of this paragraph we don't know who the people were, the people who were allegedly imprisoned illegally. Mr. President, perhaps it would be good to ask the Prosecution to be more precise, because as far as I can remember, Mr. President, the Prosecution has not been accusing people of illegal detention for reasons that they know, but that's their choice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. You may now proceed with re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Ribic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My colleague asked you whether you had the nickname Ribo and you answered that question at length. Tell me, in Mehurici at the time, was there a doctor whose name was Ribo who you did not know?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no such doctor called Ribo. There were civilians called Ribo, but they weren't doctors.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given the similarity of these family names, would it be correct to say that someone who may have testified about you might have been mistaken as far as the surnames are concerned?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's possible. The root is the same, the root of the name is the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question put to you, you also said that you didn't know who was shooting. Yesterday you said that three shells fell not far from your clinic. Tell me, do you know which positions they were fired from?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I didn't say three, I said two. One fell very near the clinic and it damaged the building and wounded three nurses of mine. The other fell about 100 metres from the building but in front of another house and the damage wasn't so extensive. These shells came from Vitez. I'm not a soldier, but we knew that these shells were HVO shells, since Vitez was in that area, or rather Mehurici is north of Vitez and as a layman I assessed that the shell or the shells had come from Vitez where HVO units were positioned, but I can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said in response to a question put to you by my learned colleague, you mentioned the population and you said that these were your assessments because you, too, were a refugee in that valley. I would like to ask you whether it would be correct to say that the population was such as it's been represented in official documents. The structure of the population corresponds to its description in the census of 1991.

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have exact information. These were rough assessments of my own. I would visit various villages, I knew which ones were Muslim villages, which ones were Catholic villages, which ones were Orthodox villages. And I knew that the majority of the population were Muslims in those villages, or rather Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To be more precise, you mainly visited the wider Mehurici sector?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You did not treat people in Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Guca Gora had their own medical corps, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't go to Brajkovici either, or Grahovcici?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't provide medical treatment there either.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to the conflict on the 8th of June you said there was shooting, and naturally you didn't know who was involved in the shooting. On the previous days, given the position of Mehurici, were you able to hear that there was shooting in some parts of the Bila Valley? And at the time did you know anything about the situation in Velika Bukovica, for example?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. There was shooting all the time and I was afraid of this shooting because in wartime people were afraid of shooting since this always heralds a large-scale conflict. So I was afraid of such shooting. I know there were celebrations of some sort of Catholic saints. I think that's when there was an attack on Mehurici. I was getting ready for an evacuation. Later I found out it wasn't an attack. I found out it was a celebration of a certain saint. I don't know the date, but later I found out that the shooting was a result of the celebration. But there was shooting at other times, too, and you really could expect other conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Doctor, I have a few minor questions to put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday with regard to a question on the mujahedin you said that the mujahedin formed a so-called unit and you said that they were joined by some young refugees. Is that in fact what you said? Could you confirm the answer you've provided to the question put to you. You said that the mujahedin were joined by young men who in your opinion were refugees. And you also said, and you mentioned the Jajce town, you said that 25.000 refugees had arrived in the area. What I would like to know is whether in your opinion, since you were in Mehurici, were there some young local men who had also joined the mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether any men from Jajce joined them. There weren't many men from Jajce in the Mehurici region. There were ten of us in total. So there weren't young men from Jajce. I mentioned 25.000 refugees. There were about 25.000 people in Jajce before the war, but some of the population had evacuated before the conflict and the attack on Jajce. So these are my assessments. I don't know the exact number of the civilians, but the column that left the town on the 27th of October, 1992, I think there were between 15 and 25.000 people in that column. They went to Travnik, to other big centres, to Zenica. Some of them went to Vitez, others to Busovaca, others to Herzegovina and Croatia. So in the mujahedin units, I don't think there were any men from Jajce whom I knew -- but wait a minute, I have just remembered something. From a village around Jajce there was someone but not in that unit, I think someone from the family called Kokici was in a unit. I know he had good logistics, that that family could get a little more food, little more parcels than the army members were able to get.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there were some young men who joined the mujahedin and you mentioned the name of a family that you could remember. And some of -- some members of this family joined the mujahedin and you said that they received food from the mujahedin. You were present at the site, as it was war -- as there was a war in country. Weren't young men obliged to join the regular BH army? Shouldn't they have been recruited? Can you explain how some young men could avoid being recruited into the regular army. How would you explain that?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do have an explanation. The state wasn't functioning under those conditions. The mobilisation was partial. Whoever would be called would report. I don't know of any cases of someone being punished for not having responded to the mobilisation. So the state wasn't functioning properly. People who were part of the Territorial Defence, they were Muslims, men of the Orthodox and Catholic faith as well. And naturally since the Territorial Defence -- well, mostly the Muslims joined the Territorial Defence but not all of the Muslims. There were very few Catholics, Orthodox men who joined the Territorial Defence. They joined national units. The army was supposed to be a Bosnian army, a multi-national army. And I must say when the Jajce Brigade was formed, I was in Mehurici at that time. I was told I would be mobilised into the Jajce Brigade because I was a refugee from Jajce. However, I didn't report but I did contact them over the phone to say that I was employed in that area. I can't really say what the procedure was if someone failed to respond to the call-up. When the state isn't functioning properly, I don't think that failing to respond to the call-up was punished. I don't know of anyone having been punished for failing to respond to the call-up. So it was up to individuals to decide whether they would free to Croatia or whether they would join army units or HVO units. Or third alternative would be to join the foreigners who were there. I don't know of any cases of someone being punished for not having responded to the mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you please clarify your administrative situation in Mehurici. According to what you said you left Jajce, you went to Travnik, and there you were told Dr. Zenic in fact took you to Mehurici where you took up your duties in the clinic. According to your answer, you had two other colleagues, there were two other doctors. You were the head doctor. What I would like to know is: When you worked in Mehurici did you receive a salary, and if so who paid you? Unless you didn't have a salary and we could understand that, too. But did you have a salary, and if so who was your employer?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I did not receive a salary. I did not have any holiday, annual leave. I was left to myself. Under such conditions, the state wasn't functioning properly, there were no salaries. And so I did not receive any remuneration. In 1994 some sort of payment or remuneration started, but 1992, 1993, you weren't receiving anything for the work you did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So you're telling us that in 1992 and in 1993 you did not receive a salary from anyone. Nobody paid you. Now, when you visited individuals who were put up in the school of Mehurici, for example, who asked you to go there? Who told you to go? Was it the military authorities or yourself? Did you spontaneously decide to go there and do a tour of duty and visit the sick and ailing? So how did that work specifically?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat. This accommodation of civilians did not come under the competency of the army, it came under the civilian protection organisation. So civilian protection had also policemen to provide security. I noticed that. So I can't give you a reason when and why I went, but I know that I went on three occasions to visit those people. The first was to see the conditions they were being put up in, to assess the conditions and whether they needed anything. And I had some people I knew there whom I socialised with before the war among the refugees. As I say, I had friends and acquaintances among the refugees. I went to visit them before the HVO conflict. They were Catholics. And then I went to see them. I used the opportunity to see and contact them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying among the people who were in the school, there were some of your acquaintances? Because you said you visited friends there. Is that right? Can you give us any names, the names of people that you knew particularly well?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not exactly. I think it was the Balta family, for example. It was a long time ago and I'm not very good with names. I meet a lot of people in the course of my work, so I'm not good a names. There's a word or name called Zastinje or something, have to do with stinje, meaning rock. It was a nice decent Catholic family and I know that I met the woman and her son and her daughter-in-law. And she asked me, Where is my Pero? So I remembered the name, my dear Pero. And I thought they had escaped. They probably had something in Travnik. I don't know what happened to them, their fate, but I know that the mother was very worried. She asked me, Doctor, where is my Pero? She said this in the friendly manner. I said I don't know, isn't he there? I said, well, Probably he escaped. So that was this exchange. It was very touching. I visited them a month ago, in fact I went to their home. I was treated very well. She was a patient of mine otherwise and her sons would bring her to see me so that I had closer contacts with them before the conflict. And it was a sort of friendly relationship that I had with the family and its members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Doctor. I myself have no further questions. Are there any additional questions? First of all, the Prosecution. Madam Benjamin, following the Judge's questions from the Bench, would you like to ask any supplementary questions of the doctor? If you do, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... with no questions, thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. What about the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Ribic, you explained in detail that you think that just the refugees from Jajce there were some members of a family connected to the mujahedin. I'm asking you now, is it true and correct that you said previously in the area there were refugees from other parts as well whom you did not know?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Certainly there were a lot of refugees not in that area but Siprage, Kotor Varos, the nearby municipalities. There were a lot of people from Banja Luka, and from Mrkonjic Grad, for example, as well as from Prijedor, Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me Doctor, please: When you spoke about those young people who were joining up with the foreigners, did you mean, did you have in mind, precisely the members of those refugees from a broader region of Krajina, not only from Jajce?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely correct. Because I said a moment ago that from the Jajce area and my own region around Mehurici as far as I knew there might have been some ten people, ten people from the Jajce region.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question, Dr. Ribic, is this: Was there - how shall I put this? - was it public knowledge or do you happen to know anything about the fact that these young people went off with these foreigners and that nobody knew where they were going and what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: ENES RIBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's absolutely correct. I didn't have an insight into that. I just saw the -- these exercises and the training that these young people underwent.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Mr. President, from us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Doctor, this brings your testimony to an end. I should like to thank you on behalf of the Trial Chamber for having to come to give testimony in The Hague. You have answered the questions put to you by the Prosecution as well as the Defence counsel and myself. I should like to wish you bon voyage back home and our best wishes for the continued success of your work as a doctor. I'm going to ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I turn towards the Defence counsel and teams. Do we have a witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like to suggest that we have an early adjournment, break. I do believe that the next witness is here but I told him to come at around 10.00. I would have to go and check to see whether the witness is indeed here and then we could continue with the examination-in-chief of the witness, if that is agreeable to the Trial Chamber as a proposal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection from the Prosecution? Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is 10 past 10.00 and we're going to take a break, a technical break, and reconvene at about 10.40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, may we have the next witness brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I should first like to check and see if you are getting the interpretation in your own language. Can you hear properly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You have been named as a witness by the Defence. Before you take the solemn declaration, I would like to ask you to give me your name and surname, date and birth and place of birth by way of introduction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Munir Karic. I live in Travnik at present, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is your date of birth and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born on the 7th of December, 1964, in the Travnik municipality, in Visnjevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is your occupation at present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have my own private company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And is it a company specialised in any particular area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transport; and part of the company is a farm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, did you occupy a post of any kind, an occupation, and if so what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 I worked as an engineer, mechanical engineer, in the Avid Lolic [phoen] mine of Travnik. I was head of the machine maintenance department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, I was a member of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a member of the army, did you have a rank of any kind, and were you assigned anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a member of the army in 1993 until the end of 1993, I was assistant commander for logistics. And towards the very end of 1993, I was the deputy commander of the 306th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Have you already time of day before an international tribunal or a national court of law with respect to the facts that took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992 and 1993, or is this the first time that you're testifying in a court of law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today's testimony is my first-time testimony about these events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Would you now take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please be seated. Before I give the floor to the Defence for their questions, since you are a Defence witness, and as you have just taken the solemn declaration you are a witness of justice, I would like to give you some information as how these proceedings will be conducted. First of all, you will be answering questions put to you by one of the two -- by the Defence counsel of one of the two accused. In general, those questions take between 45 minutes to an hour and a half. In exceptional cases, this examination can take longer. After that stage, the other Defence counsel of the other accused, if they so deem, may also ask you questions. After that we enter the next stage of the proceedings, which is the cross-examination conducted by the Prosecution. And they are seated to your right. Within the frameworks of the cross-examination, as our rules specify, rules of evidence and procedure specify, the questions are designed to test your credibility and they also have as their object to clarify some of the answers you gave to questions asked by the Defence. After that stage has been completed, the Defence counsel can also ask additional questions. The Judges sitting before you - and normally we are three but one of us is absent for professional reasons - the Judges sitting in front of you may also ask you questions at all times, if they consider this necessary. And you will see that the questions posed by the Judges are quite different to those asked by the two parties. As a general rule, we wait to ask our questions after we have heard the parties conduct their examination. So we ask questions afterwards. And the parties are of course authorised to ask additional questions, once you have supplied the Judges with answers to their questions. So those -- that is how the proceedings shall be conducted. Let us take a hypothetical. Questions might be complicated. If at any time you don't understand a question you're being asked, ask for the question to be reformulated and say whether you know or you don't know. We have no written document about your testimony, the testimony you're about to give, we don't know who you are, we don't know what facts you might have been witness to. So it is up to you to give the answers that will clarify matters for us. Everything depends on your answers, so please try and be as clear as possible, as brief as possible, and synthesise your thoughts in your answers. I should also like to tell you two additional elements of the proceedings. In addition to the fact that you were a member of the 306th Mountain Brigade, for example, you took the oath to tell the truth and the whole truth. And having taken the solemn declaration implies that you will speak the truth and not lie. If there are any lies in the course of your testimony, you must be aware of the fact that our Rules of Procedure and Evidence provide for steps to be taken for false testimony. And the penalty can go up to seven years imprisonment. In order to facilitate your testimony and have it be a truthful testimony, we have a specific rule which you will not find in other legislations and penal codes in the world and it is this. Our rules provide for the following. If you are answering a question and if in giving your answer there are elements which could one day be used against you, you must know that what you tell us here in court is covered by a form of immunity. You enjoy immunity. In American law, immunity with this hypothetical situation is granted by the Prosecution. In our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, it is the Trial Chamber who accords you this right to immunity. Therefore, I wanted to remind you of that right of yours. And this will help us Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. reach the truth and have as truthful a testimony as possible. It will allow you to speak freely and answer the questions put to you in normal fashion. If in the course of the proceedings there are any difficulties that arise, please do not hesitate to draw our attention to them. We are there to overcome any problems that might arise. So if at a certain point you have a problem, please indicate it to us, don't hesitate, and we shall resolve the issues. So in general terms, having given you those considerations, and I tell all witnesses the same thing, I hope we will have furnished the best possible conditions to hear your testimony. And we also have time constraints. So without further ado and wasting more time, I turn to the Defence and they will commence the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Karic.

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the cautions that have been given you and the information given you by the President of the Trial Chamber, I should like to ask you something myself, and that is to make pauses between my question and your answer to give the interpreters a chance to translate my question. And I shall do the same. After I hear your answer, I will pause to have your answer interpreted before asking my question which will facilitate the work of the court and everyone in court will understand what we're talking about. Do you understand, Mr. Karic?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the mechanical engineering faculty.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about your education, where you went to school, where you graduated, and when.

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: I went to primary school in Mehurici, secondary school, that is to say the Gymnasium in Travnik, and the machine engineering faculty in Zenica belonging to the Sarajevo university.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've already explained to us that at the beginning of the war you worked in Rudnik. Did you do your military service anywhere before the war, and if so which army did you serve with?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Before the war I completed by military service in the Yugoslav People's Army as a signalsman in Gornji Milanovac which is a town in Serbia. And I was there for a full 15 months doing my military service.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you gain any rank of any kind in so doing, Mr. Karic?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, do you hold a rank today?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: I was demobilised from the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina with the rank of super -- captain 1st class, and that was in the post -- and in the post-war period, I was put forward, my name was put forward for the rank of major.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war did you become a member of any political party, and if so did you hold a post with the party at all?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Before the war in 1990, in 1990 I joined the Party of Democratic Action. And at the first multi-party elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I was elected to the chamber of citizens as a delegate, as a deputy, in the republican parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, at that point in time as a delegate or deputy in the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, were you a witness of a decision taken about the future set-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: In the second half of 1991, when it came to the work of us parliamentarians, I can say it was characterised principally by the declaration that was adopted to our negotiating team led by Mr. Izetbegovic, about attempts -- over attempts to retain the then Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, with all its republics and autonomous provinces intact.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a member of the parliament, was it the position taken by the assembly that in the case that the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia could not be maintained, what the position of Bosnia-Herzegovina was to be?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Our position in the matter was quite clear. The only thing that was possible was an integral Yugoslavia with all its republics and provinces. And should any one of the republics proclaim its independence, republics that made up the Yugoslavia of the day, Bosnia-Herzegovina would follow suit; that is to say, it would proclaim its own independence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a member of parliament, were you exposed to threats at the time by certain parties in the parliament?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: I personally attended a session of the republican parliament when Karadzic, the then-president of the SDS party, threatened us, not only us individual parliamentarians, but when he threatened the entire Muslim or Bosniak people with annihilation, should they decide to opt for Bosnia-Herzegovina's independence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, Mr. Karic, did Bosnia-Herzegovina ask for its independence to be recognised, and was a demand to that effect made with the Badinter Commission which had been established?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So what was the demand made of the Badinter Commission and did the parliament respect it?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: The request and demand of the commission and the entire international community was that a referendum be conducted on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina about the republic's independence and autonomy. And the referendum was indeed held, and more than two-thirds of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina voted in favour of an independent multi-ethnic and indivisible Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When was Bosnia-Herzegovina recognised as a state, in fact? And do you know whether it became a member of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact dates of when the different countries recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina, but I know that Bulgaria was the first to recognise this and then Croatia in the month of April. We were given recognition by the United States, Germany, and finally - something that was very important for us - we were received into the United Nations family as a full-fledged member.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of all these facts, Mr. Karic, and in view of everything that took place in parliament as you said, did you remain in Sarajevo or at the beginning of the war, or rather at the beginning of April did you leave Sarajevo? And if so, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Well, prior to the outbreak of the war in the month of April, the beginning of April, I was attending a parliamentary session of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina when an attack was launched on the city of Sarajevo itself. So I managed to leave Sarajevo and reach Travnik. I was lucky in that respect because all the checkpoints -- I passed through all the checkpoints manned by the Serb aggressor and managed to return to my native village of Visnjevo in the Travnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you join the Territorial Defence, and if so, when? The Territorial Defence in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Immediately upon returning from Sarajevo, I joined the Travnik Territorial Defence, or rather I joined the Mehurici sector staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you joined the Territorial Defence, what equipment did you have to perform your duties? Did you have weapons, barracks, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Well, with your leave, I would provide you with a lengthy answer. According to the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, Defence should have been organised. We were supposed to have weapons and we were supposed to have a barracks. However, we had nothing, none of these things, because the JNA was in the barracks. And in addition to the regular units and -- many of its units from Slovenia and Croatia were moved to Bosnia-Herzegovina. And at that time certain groups also arrived from Serbia. Warehouses with weapons that belonged to the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina were mostly under the control of regular JNA units or under the control of irregular units that had started arriving at that time from Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have I understood you correctly? The Territorial Defence, and that includes your sector staff, could not receive any weapons -- any of the weapons that belonged to the Territorial Defence before the war? Is that what you have just said?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Yes. We weren't able to obtain any of these weapons. We didn't have such weapons at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, could you say how -- could you tell us how you equipped the men who reported to join the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Well, we didn't provide these men with equipment. These men found equipment for themselves. They would buy personal weapons. They would do this by selling their cows, sheep, by using some of their savings. So men who would volunteer to join the Territorial Defence obtained equipment and weapons in this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were weapons in -- openly sold or -- and if not, do you know where these people obtained the weapons that they did obtain?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Weapons were bought on the black market on the whole, and even from some Serbs who had received weapons from the Territorial Defence of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, when you joined the Territorial Defence, where was the headquarters of your sector staff at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: The headquarters of the sector staff were located in the primary school in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any duties in that sector staff?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was assigned as an assistant commander for morale.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time and later on, did the Territorial Defence, or rather the army take over control in your area and in the area of the municipality? If that is the case, please say so; and if not, can you tell me who exercised authority in that area.

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence did not assume power of any kind in that area. The civilian authorities and the military presence functioned in that area. This included all the bodies. There was a civilian protection, schools, health care, the police, or rather the MUP. All these bodies functioned at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, since you left immediately -- you left Visnjevo and you assumed your duties in the Territorial Defence, tell me whether at any point in time you noticed foreigners arriving in that area, and if so who were these foreigners?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Given that Travnik and that part of Travnik municipality was an area that a lot of refugees came to from various areas, areas where the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor had established control, there were foreigners, there were representatives of various international organisations. I also noticed the presence of some uniformed men with the insignia of the Croatian army. There were also foreigners who were Arabs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When did you first see these Arabs in the area you were in?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: I can't say when exactly, but it was towards the end of the summer and the beginning of the autumn of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, did you know where these foreigners had come from and do you know what their role was?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know exactly where these people had come from. We knew that they were Arabs since they wore their traditional clothes. Rumour had it that there were quite a few of them who had come from England and Italy, from the West. And initially according to the information I have, they said that they were representatives of humanitarian organisations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have already answered my following question when you said that they wore traditional clothes. But tell me, how did you call them? What did the people call them at the time?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Arabs and humanitarians.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, at some other period in time did the name used for these people change?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Well, later they called them mujahedin, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, you're an engineer, you're an intellectual. Did you know who the mujahedin were before the war?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: I knew nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you saw them, did you know where these foreigners first found accommodation?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't provide you with a precise answer since my duties at the time mostly involved taking care of the lines facing the Serbian aggressor on Vlasic. But according to certain information, I know that they spent some time in the Mehurici primary school and they spent some time in Poljanice. But as to where they were, the exact times they were there, I can't tell you anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally notice or did you find out from others about the attitude these foreigners, these mujahedin, had towards the local population, and who did they pay the most attention to?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning as far as I know they really acted as representatives of humanitarian organisations, and they helped the local population. Later on, according to the information I obtained, they extended the range of their activities and they started providing religious instruction for people who had joined them, who had joined them because of the material assistance offered to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, were there any organisational changes in the BH army and if so, what was your position?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: After the sector staff in Mehurici, detachments were formed and then brigades. And of the detachments in that area, the 306th Brigade was formed in November and December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From which areas did the 306th Brigade mobilise its members?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: The 306th Mountain Brigade recruited members from the former detachments in Han Bila, Mehurici, Ljuta Greda, Hum, Krpeljici - I think that's the name - and there was also a company of men who had come from Siprage, that is to say from the municipality of Kotor Varos and Skender Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, do you know whether any of the able-bodied men in that area joined any other units that were not stationed in the Bila Valley?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, the 314th Brigade and the 312th Brigade and the 17th Krajina Brigade recruited men from that area. There were also members of the 7th Muslim Brigade from that area. And naturally there were also members of other corps units and operation groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Although you have answered the Presiding Judge's question about your position, could you tell me once more: When the 306th Brigade was formed, what position did you hold?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: The 306th Mountain Brigade was formed in December. They started forming it at the end of November and finished in December 1992. And I was appointed as assistant commander for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, you have already mentioned the problems you had at the very beginning in the Territorial Defence as far as logistics is concerned. Could you now tell me, Mr. Karic, what sort of problems did you have as assistant commander for logistics in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: As I have said, the units -- the detachments, or rather the men from those detachments who joined the battalions of the 306th Mountain Brigade mostly entered the brigade with the equipment they had. The logistics supplied in the 306th Mountain Brigade were such that they didn't have any vehicles, let alone clothing, uniforms, et cetera. They didn't have everything that the logistics service of the brigade should have. And as far as the functioning of the brigade command itself is concerned, there were also problems in that it was impossible to recruit adequate professional staff for the brigade. People were assigned to certain positions in spite of the fact that they didn't have the appropriate education or the appropriate military training.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The equipment that you nevertheless obtained, ammunition and perhaps other equipment needed for defence, who did the logistics service of the 306th Brigade rely on when trying to obtain certain equipment?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: We relied on the logistics service of the 3rd Corps. However, according to the laws in force at the time, it was possible for us to obtain equipment and supplies through the War Presidency in the Travnik municipality. And I believe that in Travnik a logistics base was also formed. But all this was very symbolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the brigade did you have an area or a barracks where members of your brigade could be billeted?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: We as a brigade didn't have a barracks. All we had were buildings that had been commandeered by the department of the Ministry of Defence in Travnik. This was for the needs of the battalion and the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, you have just said that buildings for the needs of the brigade were mobilised by Travnik municipality and the secretariat for national defence. Tell me, who mobilised other equipment, for example, transport vehicles, livestock, and other items that are essential for a brigade to function in wartime conditions?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Everything that was needed was mobilised via the secretariat for defence. And only in exceptional circumstances were we able to mobilise such equipment. But this occurred quite rarely.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since in response to my previous question you said that you were a communications officer in the JNA, tell me: You or your staff in the logistics organ of the brigade, did you have the essential knowledge required to carry out these tasks?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, did anyone - and if so who? - provide you with training to enable you to carry out these tasks and were you providing with training in the course of your work and your combat?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
