utterances.text: Our brigade had an internal plan for the training of command officers and for subordinate units in their commands. And to an extent we also relied on training provided by the superior command, the command of the 3rd Corps. And we relied on our own organs, the logistics relied on the logistics organ or the operations organ in Zenica. Security would rely on the security department, et cetera. On the whole, the training was provided within the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, tell me, you in the logistics organ, were you able to provide the families of combatants with social aid, the families of combatants who had been mobilised and sent into combat?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: At that time, we didn't even have what our units needed on a daily basis. I'm referring to the units at the lines facing the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor. And as far as reserves are concerned, food, clothes, fuel, we didn't have such items for the soldiers at the lines. And in the case of the families of these soldiers, the situation was even worse.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given those problems, the fact that you couldn't provide the men with the minimum they needed to carry out their combat actions and you weren't able to provide any security for their families, given these problems, did this affect the establishment of the chain of control and command in relation to the subordinate units and troops? And if this had -- if this did have an effect on them, how did you try to deal with these problems?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time from January 1993 and for the following three or four months, there was certain problems with the HVO and members of the 306th Mountain Brigade found themselves in a specific situation. That was the case for most members of the armed forces at the time. We would send troops to the lines, and I have already mentioned the equipment we could provide them with, or rather the equipment we couldn't provide them with. And on the whole their families were provided with no food at all and with no clothes, no fuel, et cetera. So this is one of the problems I am aware of. Usually we would then discuss the matter and try to see how people go to the lines and carry out their duties there. So I can't say that there was a system of control and command in place in relation to the subordinate units, because in such conditions it was almost impossible to establish such a system. And we had to defend ourselves, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, tell me, apart from the BH army units in that area, were there any other units that were present in the same geographical area?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: In that area, apart from members of the BH army, there was the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior; there were also HVO members; there were HOS members; and there were members of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, as the assistant commander for logistics, you knew about the equipment your troops had. Were you able to observe the equipment that members of the HVO had?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I could tell when passing through checkpoints, they were as well equipped as NATO forces. That's what we said at the time. They had complete uniforms, weapons, a pistol, rifle, combat -- a full combat set, ammunition, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, at any point in time in 1993 did a conflict break out between the army and the HVO in the wider area? And if so, did that affect relations in the Bila Valley area?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Well, according to the information that we obtained, a conflict in Novi Travnik and Gornji Vakuf and in Busovaca and in Vitez broke out. These conflicts broke out at various points in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: According to what you saw and experienced, did these conflicts make part of the HVO in your area more extreme? And were there any conflicts between the army and the HVO later on?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I understood the way in which the HVO was organised at the time, the HVO was one organisation, one military unit. And naturally, HVO units behaved in the same manner. It just varied depending on the area and the time. And naturally at that time there were no open-armed conflicts with the HVO. But there were quite a few problems. As an example, HVO units became entrenched, control at checkpoints intensified, people were maltreated, people were kidnapped, intercepted, and in some cases some people were also killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Beforehand, as a proclaimed ally in the struggle against the JNA and Serb forces, in your area did the HVO in 1993 hold the front lines and defend the lines towards the Serb forces? And otherwise, do you know where their front lines were?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: The members of the HVO, as far as I know, were in a part of Vlasic, from Vlaska Gromila to the left to above the village of Velika Bukovica. They did hold a short line towards the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor, and what could be seen already at that time was that they were far behind our lines in depth towards -- on Vlasic towards the Serb aggressors. They were far is behind our backs in depth, a long way behind. And what caused great confusion and problems for us, and of course fear as well, was the fact that those lines were set up for the most part close to the villages inhabited by the Bosniak population. So we found ourselves in a situation in which individual villages or two or three villages, let's say, were completely encircled by those trenches of theirs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And where was your command, the command of the 306th Brigade, Mr. Karic?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: The command of the 306th Brigade was located in Rudnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you spoke about entrenchment and fortification on the part of the HVO forces around certain villages, tell me now, please, in relation to your command, your HQ, where were the HV [as interpreted] forces located exactly?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether they were the trenches that were dug -- well, 10 to 15 metres as the crow flies, in a straight line.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Although we have received answers to the questions I'm now going to ask you have a number of previous witnesses, I'm now going to ask you two since you were responsible for supplies. Which roads and communication lines could you reach the towns and centres of Central Bosnia in the Bila Valley, for example? How would you get there?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: They were roads running towards Travnik. So the Rudnik-Stara Bila road, Nova Bila; the Travnik junction; then from Mehurici, Guca Gora, Mostar, Gostunj, Kanare, Travnik, Zenica. The Han Bila-Ovnak road, Zenica. Cajdras, Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On page 48, line 10, my question was: In relation to your command where were the HVO forces, the Croatian defence council forces, the HVO. Whereas in the transcript it says the HV which means the Croatian army. But your answer was HVO?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Yes, HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for that interruption. Tell me, please, what happened in 1993 with those roads, those lines of communication. And how could the population and army communicate with Travnik and Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: In 1993, or rather in the first half of 1993 checkpoints were erected along those roads, and I've already said that they were manned by the HVO and HOS and sometimes members of the Croatian army, the HV as well. And they would have insignia of the HV, the Croatian army. Now, whether they were or not, I can't say. They had that insignia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, in addition to setting up these checkpoints, was there anything in the conduct of the HVO which led to conflicts or humiliation or what happened along those roads? Anything like that as a result of the erection of those checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Well, I can give you my own experience, what I experienced myself passing through those checkpoints as a logistics man. There were precarious situations. We would be searched, provoked. You never knew when you would be allowed to pass a checkpoint and reach your superior command with a vehicle carrying the goods you needed, both on the road to Zenica and on the road to Travnik. According to what I heard -- or rather I experienced one situation. I was in the command when a group of our officers arrived and I would say they had -- how shall I put this? It wasn't humiliation. But let me use the term "humiliation," for want of a better one. They were disarmed. They took their clothes off, anything that was of any value. They took their trainers. I even heard that they were forced to eat grass, to graze.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So all these provocations --

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: May I be allowed to finish? All this happened perhaps 150 to 200 metres from the HQ headquarters, the brigade's headquarters, what these people had experienced and been put through.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So in addition to what you have just said witnesses testified to a number of situations, but I'm asking you since you were a member of the command of the 306th Brigade whether your own brigade had received any orders to retaliate in equal force, or did you behave differently? Was your conduct different trying to avoid a conflict? So can you tell me what you know about that? What would you say?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: What I can tell you is this: We -- as I was saying, what I can tell you is this: We as the brigade's command had strict orders at all Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. costs to try to avoid any conflicts with the HVO and to try to establish maximum cooperation through negotiations with their representatives, with the representatives of their own HQ. So in that respect I remember that some commissions were set up for permanent cooperation and contact with representatives of their brigades. And they have the task of touring their units as well as our own units so that the trenches and communicating trenches were filled in.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you -- were you, Mr. Karic, faced with reaction on the part of the fighters to this absolutely peaceful attitude and position that was taken? Even when the greatest humiliations were inflicted, there was always the desire to avoid conflict?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Everything that was happening both to our brigade headquarters and command and everything that was happening in Vitez and Busovaca and so on certainly gave rise to bitterness among the member of the 306th Mountain Brigade. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Prosecution just would like to intervene regarding the last question. My learned friend has used the word "greatest humiliations were inflicted." And insofar, this question was leading. The witness has already answered but the Prosecution just wants to put this on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Defence has taken note of that, I gather.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. I apologise for my qualifications of the events that were recounted by the witness himself. I will do my best to avoid any leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, the overall relationships that you have described and recounted, did they and in what way, if so, affect the work of the command and its deployment and distribution in the area?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Everything that was happening during that period of time had a highly negative impact on the unit's development -- the unit's organisation, the command, and the unit itself, the men -- so that our brigade during this period of time, instead of moving forwards in the military sense, it was faced with a situation in which it receded in all respects. And we as the command were not in a position to rally our forces, to gather in full strength.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, where were you at the beginning of June 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of June 1993, I was engaged in touring the area, gravitating towards the Serb and Montenegrin aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you went on assignment, where were you in actual fact? Which battalion? Where were you?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Upon my return from a tour of duty and touring the area, I wasn't able to reach the command HQ and I was in Mehurici, the headquarters of the 2nd Battalion in fact -- or rather, the 1st Battalion. I apologise for that slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the commander of the brigade was at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: As far as we knew, he was in Krpeljici, the commander, in an encirclement. And as we asked the commander to come out and with the help of the UNPROFOR of the day, that was not -- just not possible, even with UNPROFOR's help.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So who stayed at Rudnik, at the brigade headquarters in the command?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, in the brigade command the assistant commander for security stayed on, for security, signals, and part of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karic. Let me go back a bit to a previous question that we -- a matter that we discussed at the beginning of the examination-in-chief, and that is the appearance of these foreigners. And in answers one of my questions about them, you said that certain problems arose principally because of the way they were being trained -- trained them in practicing their religion, in their religious rites. Tell me, please, the position of these humanitarians, if I can put it that way, who brought about -- who led to excesses with respect to practicing religion. Did that have an adverse effect on the Bila Valley? Did certain problems arise and whether and in what way did the 306th Brigade confront these problems?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: These problems grew from one day to the next. The way in which they tried on our own terrain to introduce this new way of practicing religion was for the vast majority of the population just unacceptable. So that from that angle of vision we experienced problems everywhere -- with our places of religious worship, in the mosques, for example, in our daily communication, daily lives. So this was an enormous problem which really did upset the morale of our members. Furthermore, we had situations in which a number of people whom we were not able to mobilise even under state organs and place under our own command [as interpreted]. And at that time, the people lived fairly well. Their families were well taken care of. When I say "fairly well," their families had a means of livelihood, whereas our members in that respect were in a very poor state, catastrophic in fact, just like their families. So it was difficult to explain to members of the 306th Mountain Brigade how people could behave that way without you being able to do anything about it. And that people didn't want to go up to the front line, whereas the members of the 306th had to spend several days and perhaps several weeks up at the front line without knowing what was happening to their families and what would happen to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, during that period of time were you witness to certain family ties between those foreigners and certain families in the area, whether they were the local population or the people who had come into your area as a result of the war?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Well, already at that time, during that period, they expanded their activities -- actually, they married our girls. They were very young girls usually. And from our point of view and the way we lived our lives in the area, this was quite unacceptable. Because if a girl of 13, 14 married somebody who was 30 -- you can imagine how bitter the population was for the most part when they saw things like that taking place. Then there were other situations, for example the sister or relative of one of our members was married, for example, to a foreigner. And that led to problems, too. So these were very serious problems and problems that just couldn't be solved.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to June 1993 for a moment now, please. As you happened to find yourself in the command and headquarters of the 1st Battalion with some other member of the command, did you at some point in time at the beginning of June receive demands from the commander, receive a request from the commander? And what did you learn about what was happening in other areas of the Bila Valley?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: We did receive a request from the commander and members of the command who were with the command in Krpeljici to the effect that we ought to help the population of Velika Bukovica. And different information was coming in, but according to all the information, the situation was serious. The population seemed to have been killed, burnt, that some of them had been taken to camps, and so on and so forth. And it became clear to us at the time that in fact the HVO was applying tactics which had been applied up until then. It was negotiating on the one hand until it brought us into a situation where the brigade command and the brigade itself was mostly disbanded and in 80 per cent of the cases found itself in total isolation under siege. And when the brigade found itself in a situation of that kind, the HVO then proceeded to undertake ethnic cleansing of that part of the Travnik municipality in a place called Velika Bukovica. And something similar happened in Busovaca and Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you try and reach those fighters and the people of Velika Bukovica to help them out?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: The wish was there. Once we received all that information, it was our desire to help the people. And as far as I know some of our men were supposed to go to Velika Bukovica. However, on the one hand we had the HVO front lines and above us we had the Serb and Montenegrin aggressor lines. We were surrounded. So we failed in that attempt.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the military situation that ensued and that the situation you yourselves were in, nonetheless at a point in time were some free units from Mehurici able to start out and undertake combat activities and what happened?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were faced with a situation like that. A number of men from the 306th Brigade from Velika Bukovica reached Mehurici and broke -- breaking through the HVO lines. And then we received information as to what was actually happening there. And what happened was what we were told. Some of the people were killed, some elderly persons were set fire to in their own homes. And all the rest who were there, all the other people, were taken off. At that point in time we heard they were being taken to Nova Bila. After that some of our units set out in an attack towards the HVO lines. What I want to say is this: Before that -- or rather, the night before -- the night before the attack, the night before the fighting, Mehurici was exposed throughout the night to shelling. And that had never happened yet. The shelling came from the HVO lines and their positions, their artillery weapons, and also from the Serbs and Montenegrin aggressors, their lines. And this served to confirm the thesis that the HVO units and the units of the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressors were working in cohorts. They were coordinated and had been for some time, and were preparing an attack on the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, Mr. Karic, in view of the fact that you yourself happened to be in Mehurici during that -- if I can put it this way -- counterattack and the general fighting in the Bila Valley, what did you yourself do? What were your tasks and assignments faced with that kind of situation?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: As assistant commander for logistics for the most part I did what I could to take care of the wounded combatants who came in that day. We were not able to see to our fallen fighters, those who had been killed. We had a lot of problems in caring for the wounded and how to provide transport for them to the Zenica hospital. We ourselves were not able to transport them to Travnik. So the transport to Zenica didn't follow the lines and roads against Ovnak. We had to drive them across the hill, so that the journey lasted a long time. And if the person was lucky and was transported in a motor vehicle, then it would take four or five hours. If he had to be transported in a horse-drawn cart or something like that, then it would take all day for a wounded person to reach the Zenica hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a member of the command of the 306th Brigade, when did you first encounter other members of the command? When did you meet up with them first?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: I met up with them first, with other members of the command -- well, as I set off in the afternoon against Hum hill, it was only towards evening that I met the command of the 306th Brigade. In the meantime, I received information that my uncle on my mother's side had died in the fighting in the Travnik municipality, in Dolac. And then that night I returned to Visnjevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, while you were going about your business and assignments, tell me please, in Mehurici did you happen to notice or learn that some civilians from Croatian villages had been brought in? And if so, if you learnt about that, do you know what happened to those people? And did you also learn of some other pieces of information about a possible crime that might have taken place during those combat operations?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Prosecution has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The Prosecution objects against this question. It's a compound question. There are actually a couple of these questions. And in addition, my learned colleague is leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Try and break the question up into several parts, please, because if we look at that question and the lines, there are several subquestions, if I can put it that way, within the overall question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, you have understood the objections made by the Prosecution. Let me ask you first: While you were in Mehurici on that particular day, did you learn that people had been brought into Mehurici, civilians from certain -- some Croatian villages?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know or did you know what village they were brought in from and why?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: At that moment what I learnt was this: They were people, according to information received from members of our brigade who were bringing them in, they were from the village of Maline mostly. They were brought in to Mehurici exclusively for security and safety reasons, because the fighting during the day had become fierce, there was heavy fighting, and different information was coming in and reports, not only from our own terrain but from the broader area of the Travnik municipality about the fighting. So that for safety and security reasons, those people who were brought in -- well, that's the reason why they were brought to Mehurici in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, did you have any obligations with respect to these individuals?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Since they had been taken to the 1st Battalion command, the command of the 1st Battalion assumed responsibility for the people who were taken to the Mehurici primary school.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whose duty and obligation it was to provide them with food and to provide them with conditions in which they could live?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Well, as I have said, as far as the living conditions and food are concerned, it's the 1st Battalion command, or rather its bodies cooperating with the bodies of civilian protection that were supposed to take care of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me whether on that day before you went to Krpeljici you found out that a crime might have been committed.

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: From the men who had escorted these inhabitants, I heard that some of the prisoners had been taken from them. But at that time they didn't know what had happened to them. That's what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you later obtain any other information concerning these people who had been kidnapped, the people who were being escorted by members of the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Later at meetings of the brigade command, I obtained certain information, just like all the other members of the brigade command, according to which it was possible that a crime had been committed there, and that the people who had been kidnapped from members of our brigade's 1st Battalion had perhaps been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who provided that information at the meeting of the command?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: I think it was the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, did the security organ mention any measures that had been taken in order to shed light on the event?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Naturally, the security organ should have taken certain measures in order to find out what had happened there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, could you please tell me when you returned from Visnjevo, where your uncle was buried after he had been killed, did you find out anything about what had happened in Guca Gora, that is to say in the monastery in Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: I also obtained information as a member of the brigade command, according to which there had been problems in relation to the protection of the monastery in Guca Gora. And according to what was said at the time, it appears that Commander Sipic and Commander Alagic as well as the assistant commander for morale in the 306th, I think his name was Halim Husic, it seems that they were able to protect the monastery in Guca Gora from certain individuals. They prevented it from being desecrated and destroyed, et cetera. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, given the threat to the monastery were any measures taken within the brigade to ensure that protection was provided for the monastery?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: At that time our military police platoon was securing the monastery. Later on when I assumed the post of the command of the 306th Mountain Brigade, we relocated the brigade command in order to protect the monastery because as our duties increased, wasn't sure -- we weren't sure that the military police would be able to protect the monastery at all times. So we managed to protect this monastery because we were aware of what it meant for our history, of its historical significance, and we were aware the consequences of its destruction might have.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, how far away were the combat lines with the HVO? How far away from Guca Gora and the monastery were the combat lines facing the HVO? And I'm referring to the period after the event that took place on the 8th of June.

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Well, they were about 2 kilometres away as the crow flies, so within the range of small calibre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you witness the area of Guca Gora coming under the attack and any buildings or facilities in Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did witness a mortar attack on the monastery in Guca Gora. This was an HVO attack. Luckily some of the military policemen survived. These were policemen who were in part of the monastery -- who were staying in part of the monastery.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When that shell fell on the monastery, did the army take any measures in relation to that act? And if so, what sort of measures did it take?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: To the extent that this was possible, we managed to repair the roof and the walls and to make it look fairly normal.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: According to some of the witnesses, the monastery was handed over to those to whom it belonged again, to priests -- to the priests from that monastery. Tell me, do you know when this took place and how the monastery was returned to these people?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: I was personally present when the monastery was handed over to these people, to members of the clergy. I know that at the request of the church, we soon left the monastery. The command and its attached units left and relocated. And when handing the monastery over to these people, there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was the monastery intact and what did members of the clergy tell you at the time? Did they have any comments to make, any objections to raise? Did they express their opinions on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: When the monastery was handed over to them, they didn't have any objections to raise; on the contrary, they thanked us for what we had done and they congratulated us. That's what they did, literally.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just have a few more questions. You said that you found out that these HVO members had been kidnapped, HVO members escorted by members of the 306th Brigade. Did you find out who kidnapped those HVO members?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Well, according to the information we had, the HVO members were kidnapped by members of the mujahedin detachment. And perhaps there was some local people accompanying them as well. That's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was it possible to find out who these local people were? Did they conceal their identity in some way or was it possible to find out who they were?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: If it had been possible, we would have discovered their identity. As far as I know, although this was the duty of a different organ in the brigade, in spite of all the attempts we made to find out about this, to find out who these people were, we were unable to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, since you were the assistant commander for logistics, tell me whether the mujahedin provided logistics support for the 306th Brigade and for you as the assistant commander of logistics.

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As assistant commander for logistics, did you provide certain equipment and logistics support for those foreigners who were in Poljanice?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: We couldn't even provide our units with logistics support, let alone anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a member of the 306th Brigade command, do you know whether at any time in 1993 these foreigners were placed under the command of the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: There were never any foreigners in the 306th Mountain Brigade. I'm not aware of them ever being placed under the command of the 306th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After these events and after the combat operations in June, did you and in brigade come across incidents of looting? And if so, do you know what measures were taken?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: I can only tell you what I found out from other organs, at meetings, et cetera. The brigade was in such a situation that its defence lines were not only doubled but it had even more defence lines than that. As I said, military police had certain duties, they had to protect the Guca Gora monastery, they had to protect certain families that had stayed on, families of Croatian nationality that had stayed on after the fighting. People did speak about looting; I don't know how extensive this was, but I do know that we all did everything we could at the time to prevent such incidents from occurring.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, in such a vast and inaccessible area, the organs that informed you about the measures that were taken, did they also inform you and did you personally know what sort of difficulties these military police organs faced when trying to determine the identity of the people involved in looting?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, according to the information I have obtained from other organs at briefings, I know that there are many people in that area who weren't originally from Travnik municipality but they had been expelled from areas under the control of the Serbian aggressor. Furthermore, some people came from municipalities that had been ethnically cleansed by the HVO. And then in that area there were members of many units, the 314th, the 17th, members of the 7th Muslim Brigade who were on leave, members of units attached to the staff, and so on. So when certain perpetrators were indicated, sometimes such perpetrators had two or three identity cards. Naturally, we tried to establish the identity of each brigade member on the basis of papers, but problems occurred. I wasn't able to ensure that everyone had photographs and had these identity cards. So there were problems; that's certain. But as far as members of the 306th at that time are concerned, I assume that the security organ was functioning properly and members of -- a lot of members of the 306th Brigade were detained to the extent that this was possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's 20 past 12.00. We'll have a break and we will resume at about 10 to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm turning to the Defence to see if they have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have a few questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karic, in the course of your testimony you said in 1993 you were the assistant commander for logistics. And towards the end of 1993 you were the deputy commander, in fact. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: When performing those duties at that period, I assume that you had contact with and knew which BH army units were in the Bila Valley.

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Well, I should have known.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned the formation of units and brigades and you mentioned men from the Bila Valley who joined various BH army units, I think it's page 42 of the transcript, you said that they were recruited into 312th, 314th, the 17th Krajina Brigade, the 306th Brigade, and you said that individuals also joined the 7th Brigade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: When you said individuals, could you tell us what you meant by individuals exactly.

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Men who were liable for military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Were there a few people who joined this brigade than men who entered the 312th, 306th, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Yes. This concerned a very small number of men.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: A very small number of men?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: A very small number of men joined the 7th Muslim Brigade. I'm referring to men from the Bila Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, there were no organised units in the Bila Valley, in the establishment sense, there were no organised units?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: As far as I know I don't think there was an organised formation of the 7th Muslim Brigade in the Bila Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Let's now go back to the 8th of June, or rather to the beginning of June 1993. You've already answered a question put to you by my colleague Ms. Residovic, and at the time you said you were in the command of the 1st Battalion in Mehurici. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question put to you by Ms. Residovic, you said that some of your units after returning from Bukovica launched a counterattack in the direction of the HVO lines. You were referring to units of the 306th Brigade, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, on the day we have spoken about, the 7th and 8th of June, 1993, when you were in the 1st Battalion command in Mehurici, according to the information you have there are no members of the 7th Brigade in Mehurici at the time who may have participated in the combat operations?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no such members.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll turn to the Prosecution now, who may conduct their cross-examination. We have another 45 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Good morning, Witness. My name is Mathias Neuner. I'm putting a couple of questions to you and in case you don't understand the question, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. please ask me to rephrase it or ask it in another way and I will try to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, you testified you were a member of the SDA. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You were also a member of the SDA main board; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: No, it's not correct. I was a member of the parliament. I was in the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And sometimes I attended meetings of the main committee of the SDA. As a member of the parliament, I wasn't a member of the main board of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understand. As a non-member of the SDA main board you attended meetings of the SDA. For example, in November 1993, did you attend such a meeting in Zenica, a meeting of the SDA main board?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but that's possible. I'm not sure, but perhaps I did attend that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Did you attend any meetings of the SDA main board in Central Bosnia? Do you remember attending any of the meetings in Central Bosnia in 1993, late 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall the dates and places, but if you have certain knowledge as to when that was, what the topic was at the main board meeting, then I can tell you whether I was there or not, because my attendance at the main board meetings was not compulsory. However, if you have any knowledge pointing to the fact that I was there, please go ahead and ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'll switch the topic. If I may go to August 1993. In August 1993, were you attending a session of the RBiH Assembly? Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Whenever I was able to attend meetings of the RBiH Assembly I did so. Now, it's the same as with the other case, records and minutes were kept of the people attending the assemblies. I would be unless I was prevented from doing so. Was that a session in Sarajevo? Is that the one?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I have looked at a document indicating to me that in August 1993 you attended such a session. At this moment I cannot tell you exactly where the meeting was. I just had your name mentioned on the -- on one of the minutes of the assembly session. I'll switch to another topic. I switch --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What objection do you have, Counsel? Don't forget that the cross-examination is there to test the credibility of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no problems with that, Your Honour. The witness would have to show documents or be shown documents to refresh his memory. The Prosecution should show him documents to refresh his memory, otherwise there's no point in checking it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Prosecution, would they like to respond? Do you have a document to present to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a document to present to this witness, but not in relation to his political career. I just thought as an opening question I could ask this question. But as I indicated earlier, I'm prepared to switch to questions relating to the military career, which I will do now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You were appointed as assistant commander for --

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: If I might be -- I do apologise. But may I -- may I make a comment? Sometimes I wasn't able to attend one parliamentary session or three. I just can't remember the dates. But I did do my best to attend parliamentary sessions regularly, because it was the parliament of my own country, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understand that. Thank you. Turning to your appointment as assistant commander for logistics for the 306 Brigade. You were appointed in March 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: I was appointed to assistant commander for logistics of the 306th Brigade in the month of November or December, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Just to refresh your memory, may I ask the usher to distribute a new document, with the Trial Chamber's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, the Defence notes that this is a new document which is neither on the list of documents put forward by the Prosecution at the beginning of the case nor a document admitted into evidence during the presentation of evidence. So we should like to address the Chamber without the witness's presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Usher, would you escort the witness out of the courtroom for a few minutes until we deal with the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have the floor, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The question that we'd like to address is the use of documents by the Prosecution during the presentation of Prosecution -- of evidence put forward by the Defence, in the Defence case. Documents that can be used by the Prosecution is regulated by Article 65 ter (E)(iii), Rules of Procedure and Evidence. And according to 65 ter (E)(iii), the Prosecution must supply the Defence first of all with a list of all the exhibits that it intends to use during the case and to give a copy of the same to the Defence. We submit, respectfully, that this procedure is directly related to Article 21, paragraph 4(A) of the Statute of the international Tribunal, which states that it is the right of an accused to be fully informed of the nature and details of the charges brought against him at the earliest opportunity. And one wonders, Mr. President, whether this was carried out and that on two levels: first of all, so that the accused should not be taken by surprise in preparing his defence case; and secondly, Mr. President, that the accused could have enough time and the means necessary to prepare his defence. The case before the international Tribunal is divided into two parts. First of all, you have the presentation of evidence put forward by the Prosecution, that is to say the Prosecution case; and then a second stage, the Defence case where the representatives of the accused put forward their case. The division of the trial into two parts is not a question of common law or civil law, it is rather a question of the Rules and Statute of the international Tribunal. And after the Prosecution case has been put forward, we suggest, Mr. President, that the accused has to know all the charges that have been made against him, and that the Prosecution cannot divide its case in such a way by showing certain documents during the Prosecution case and keeping back reserve documents, additional documents, that it will bring out in due course, because that will be in violation of the principle of a Prosecution case recognised by the European human-rights court. So, Mr. President, we once again ask ourselves what the purpose was for dividing these two parts, as it is the right of the accused to remain silent, and more importantly, if there is no proof at the end of the presentation of the Prosecution case, the accused -- it is not up to the accused to present a defence if a case hasn't been made. If there -- a case has been moved according to the Chamber's ruling on a motion following Article 98 bis of the Rules of Procedure, the accused is then required to present his defence case. And one asks what the position is, of the Prosecution doing that Defence case presentation. So one must understand the position of the accused during that second stage, and it would be useful to look at the equality of arms question in this regard. And I submit respectfully, Mr. President, that the equality of arms before the International Criminal Tribunal, just like before all other penal courts does not imply that the parties have the same status or play the same role or have the same reason for being a case before the international Tribunal. You have the Prosecution and its role, which is to set forth a theory for accusing and charging the accused. And the accused has to -- the burden of proof is on the part of the Prosecution and not on the accused. So we must ask ourselves what the role and status of the accused is. It is, first of all, the presumption of innocence and the right to carry out a full defence case, present a full defence case. So the equality of arms, in our opinion, Mr. President, means that the two parties should have the means to fulfil their respective roles and differing roles. That is what we believe to be the substance of the equality of arms, which brings us back to the position of the accused -- and the Prosecution. The Prosecution has charges against two accused. They have had five years to investigate and present all the elements in the Prosecution case. In -- and if there are some new facts that come to light in the course of the second stage of the trial, that is to say during the Defence case, the rules provide relying on Article 85(A)(3)(i) that the Prosecution has the right to reply. And this right to reply can mean calling new witnesses. The Prosecution can call new witnesses and also present new evidence in rebuttal. So when the Defence case goes ahead in the second stage, this is not the moment when the Prosecution can bring up new documents. And in conclusion, Mr. President, it is the position of the Defence with respect to the principles I have just referred to that during the cross-examination, we submit, Mr. President, the Prosecution can of course utilise documents that have already been admitted into evidence. Moreover, there is no obligation on the part of the Prosecution to give us full notice of those documents because we already have them all; they have already been tendered. However, we should like to note that in order to have fair play prevail, we always like to inform the Prosecution of the documents that we ourselves are going to use with the witnesses that are to be heard in the Defence case. And we would like to hope that we would be given the same treatment by the Prosecution, because the obligations that rest on the Defence are to supply all the documents to the Prosecution, which is something which we have done in major part. It is an ongoing process, of course, and every time we have a witness we inform the Prosecution of the documents that we shall be utilising, which we are not obliged to do if we follow the letter of the rules. The second source of documents that can be used during a cross-examination are documents which have not been admitted into evidence but which existed on the original list of the Prosecutor, that is to say the list presented during -- on the basis of the pre-trial process and Rule 65 ter. Therefore, Mr. President, we feel that if the Prosecution would like to use a document that comes under that section they are free to do so, but they must inform us in advance. They themselves have to prepare the document and we can discuss the document with the accused. The most important question, Mr. President, has to do with new documents, ones that have not been exhibited and have not been included on the Prosecutor's list. And those documents, Mr. President, we submit cannot be utilised by the Prosecution during the Defence case unless, of course, they have applied to the Chamber to do so and have the documents added to their list, explaining why they were not able to come by those documents earlier on. So the new documents that we referred to had to do with the Prosecution's case and the motion that it has been pending for five years, especially after the Prosecution case has been concluded. And that is the Prosecution's prerogative. We should also like to say, Mr. President, those documents should be supplied in rebuttal, and when the Prosecution comes up with new documents and when it knows that it would like to utilise those documents at all stages of the Defence case, the document must be divulged, disclosed, to the Defence teams. Having said that, Mr. President, there is always an exception and we can understand that an exception can be made. If a witness was mentioned by the Prosecution, the Prosecution can then move to discredit the witness, attack his credibility, and impeach him. And in order to do so, perhaps they need a precise, specific, document, where a lie was stated on the part of an individual. And in that case, we would never prevent the Prosecution from shattering the credibility of the witness. Of course, we always believe our witnesses to be credible, but we can always be surprised in the opposite direction, as has been the case in previous instances. So I think that the positions of the Prosecution and the Defence teams are different. It is the Prosecution who has the burden of proof, and we have the presumption of innocence and rights derived from that fact. So we should like to ask that if new documents are being utilised that they should be presented to the Trial Chamber first in a motion explaining why they were not able to be presented earlier on, as provided for by the rules and regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm now going to give the floor to the Prosecution, but let me summarise. The problem which was raised by the Defence is the following: The Defence has noted that the document which the Prosecution wishes to produce was not disclosed to the Defence in keeping with Article 66 or Rule 66 and Rule 68 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the Tribunal. And that therefore it is a new document and must be considered as such, a completely new document which the Defence has suddenly discovered today. Now, the Defence says that since it is a new document, the Prosecution always has the possibility of introducing the document once the stage of Rule 85 allows the Prosecutor to enter into rebuttal. And then the Prosecution can bring in new witnesses and supply a new list of exhibits containing new documents. But in the stage in which the Defence has been disclosed the majority of the documents, it is no longer possible for the Prosecution to bring up new documents, except, as the Defence has said, given a hypothetical, in a hypothetical case where the Prosecution has proof or elements allowing it to conclude that the witness is lying. Now, in that hypothetical case, then it must inform the Defence thereof and inform the Trial Chamber above all, so that we can discuss the matter. So at this stage the Defence is assuming that the document produced was not one that was on the list of exhibits provided by the Prosecution and it objects to it. So I think that I have precised and summarised the position taken by the Defence earlier on. We should like to have a response from the Prosecution with respect to the possibility on the part of the Prosecution of producing a new document, what they have to say, and put it to a witness during the examination of a Defence witness. I'm going to give you the floor, and of course we should like to know -- you will be hearing whether you can use the document or not. If it is a complex matter, you might like to give your answer in due course, at some later date.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, you took the words out of my mouth. I was just about to ask the Chamber to give the Prosecution some time so as to review this matter. But I wish to say on behalf of the Prosecution team and the Prosecution that I represent, the Prosecution is in no way - and I would like to assure my colleagues - in no way intends to ambush the Defence in any way. I think somewhere along the line there might have been a misinterpretation with respect to the disclosure, and I write it down to inexperience, perhaps on the part of this Prosecution team. And in light of that I wish to apologise if in fact that is what the Defence thinks the Prosecution has set out to do. And we would ask the Trial Chamber to allow us some time within which to respond. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll give you the floor again in a minute. The Prosecution has said that they will respond to this legal issue that you have raised, but they need time. The Prosecution claims that they did not want to put the witness into any difficulties. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Very rapidly: I wouldn't want the Prosecution to have the impression that we thought they were trying to lay an ambush for us. We just claim that according to the rules, documents should be filed before the trial and if new documents arrive in the course of the procedure -- in the course of the trial, this should be dealt with then. There are certain rules to be followed. With regard to the Defence's arguments, you mentioned the Rules 66 and 68 of the rules. Mr. President, according to Rule 66, this is a rule that concerns the pre-trial phase. And because of Rule 65, this rule is no longer in force. Rule 65 concerns the exhibits that the Prosecution wants to tender into evidence. Rule 68 is always applicable as soon as the Prosecution has exculpatory documents. These documents should be provided to us. This is done on a continual basis by the Prosecution. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Defence counsel for the other accused, is there anything you would like to say about the legal issue? Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If I can support the submissions that have been made by Mr. Bourgon, there's nothing further to add on those. Other than in respect to this particular document itself, which is an order from the supreme command staff. It's another one of the documents that comes from the command staff in Sarajevo. There was a previous document a few weeks ago that fitted into the same category which was not admitted into evidence, primarily because the witness concerned at that stage wasn't able to identify the document in any way. And our submission in relation to this particular document would be precisely the same, that the witness concerned, mainly involved the 306 command, is not going to be in a position to comment on a document that comes from the supreme command, which in fact was signed by the supreme chief Mr. Sefer Halilovic. And the Prosecution might seek to suggest that because there's certain information in the document or because the witness is named in the document that he might have something to say about it. In our submission, that is the wrong approach to take. If there is something which the Prosecution wish to ask the witness about which might be mentioned in the document, they can do that through their examination. They needn't show a document to a witness simply because his name is mentioned in it. If there are to be connections made between what a witness says and a particular document, those can always be done at the appropriate stage, which is when the Prosecution present their closing argument. So if our submission the Prosecution should only put documents to the witness where they are able to identify the document and be able to comment on the contents of the document, but not simply because there might be some connection to the witness concerned. So our objection remains the same as for the previous document and for all the more general reasons that Mr. Bourgon has outlined. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: May I ask the Prosecutor, do you want to submit the document to test the credibility of the witness or has it a different purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document was an appointment order. This witness was, according to the document, being appointed on the 12th of March, 1993, to the position of assistant commander for logistics in the 306 Brigade. And the reason why I wanted to put it to him, and I actually stated it on the record, was that I wanted to refresh his memory with regard to the dates. Secondly, this document in B/C/S and English had been disclosed in advance to the Defence yesterday afternoon, and there is no procedural unfairness, insofar that this was advanced notice. And the reason why this document was or would have been put to the witness would just have been to refresh him with regard to the actual appointment. And that the appointments within the ABiH are made by the supreme command is certainly true -- and since it was raised here by my learned colleague. But the Prosecution believes that since our witness has been appointed on the 12th of March, 1993, he must have received one way or the other an appointment or a notification of this appointment order. So for the very fact that -- so it was not intended to put the witness in any embarrassing situation at all, just on the contrary: to refresh his knowledge with regard to certain events which are -- which have been in the past which are 11 years -- which have taken place 11 years ago. And the Prosecution actually intended to help this witness in refreshing his memory. And the document, as I said, has been disclosed to the Defence yesterday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Given the issue that has been raised, we will withdraw to discuss the issue and we will return very soon. --- Break taken at 1.31 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber has discussed the matter to see whether the Prosecution can show this witness the document to refresh the witness's enemy -- memory. Since the Defence has raised a legal issue that concerns the disclosure of new documents and since the Prosecution wants time to respond to this legal issue, the Trial Chamber believes that the Prosecution should not show this document to the witness at this stage. And naturally, the Chamber will render its decision on the issue raised once the Prosecution has informed us of its position. We will now continue with the hearing. We'll call the witness back into the courtroom and you may continue with your cross-examination, but you should not show the witness this document which we will return to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: The Prosecution is obliged to the Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you please state again when you were appointed to the position of assistant commander of this 306 Brigade, in what month.

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Well, I performed the duties of the assistant commander for logistics in the 306th Brigade from the time when the brigade was formed. That was in November or December 2000 -- I apologise, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And you testified that in April 1993 you were arriving from Sarajevo -- no. Excuse me. In April 1992 you were arriving from Sarajevo to the area of Travnik; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: I wasn't permanently present in Sarajevo. I resided in the municipality of Travnik, where I had a full-time job. In April 1992 I came from Sarajevo to the municipality of Travnik, to the village of Visnjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: As assistant commander for logistics in the 306 Brigade, to whom did you report? Who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: My superior as assistant commander for logistics was the commander of the 306th Mountain Brigade -- that's as far as commanding is concerned. But I had constant contact with the logistics in the 3rd Corps, and mostly with the operations organ in the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: What was the name of your superior and your other superior in the 3rd Corps logistical organ in spring 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: I only had one superior, that was the commander of the 306th Mountain Brigade. In November 1993, is that your question? Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I wanted to know from you in spring 1993 to whom in the 3rd Corps did you send reports? Who was the person in the 3rd Corps to whom you sent reports?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Well, this question is a little different from the previous one, at least the way in which I understand it. My request in terms of logistics of the 306th Brigade were made to the logistics service in the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You stated that outside your direct area of responsibility, there was also logistical base in Travnik, if I remember correctly. Within the 3rd Corps area, were there other logistical -- logistic bases, do you remember, in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: I'd like to clarify this, too. In wartime conditions and when there is an imminent threat of war, all state organs were obliged to do everything they could so that units of the BH army, that is to say the armed forces of the BH Republic, could be fully functional. And it's in that sense that I spoke about the logistics base in Travnik. Whether it was the War Presidency or whether there was some sort of logistics base there, I wouldn't go into that now. As for your own question you asked whether there was another logistics base or any other logistic bases in our zone of responsibility. What do you mean when you say "in our zone of responsibility"?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I assume that you stationed supplies for your troops somewhere in the area of responsibility of the 306 Brigade. Where were such logistical posts or logistical bases within the 306 Brigade, if I start here?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: During which period?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let me clarify a few things. As I have already said, I've told you about the supplies we had when answering a question put to me by Ms. Residovic. We didn't have a lot of supplies; we had almost no supplies. This varied depending on the brigade concerned. The 306th Mountain Brigade had a mountain post in Rudnik, and that is where I was positioned. Each battalion command also had its command post and they had warehouses there. And most of the supplies we had -- well, we had very few reserve supplies and often we had no supplies, but these supplies, the ones that we had, were on the lines, they were kept on the lines. When we only had a front facing the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor, that's where these supplies were kept and that's the zone of responsibility of the 306th Brigade. And when the problems arose with the HVO, when a conflict broke out with the HVO, we then had all the logistics supplies in the area of the lines. So with regard to the 306th Brigade's zone of responsibility, you can't say the command is in Rudnik and then there is a battalion in Krpeljici, et cetera. You can't say that that's the zone of responsibility of the 306th Brigade. That wasn't the zone of responsibility of the 306th Brigade. Our zone of responsibility was the front line, first of all. The front line facing the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor. We know where the 306th Brigade held the lines. And later, when fighting broke with the HVO, our zone of responsibility was the front line facing the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The 1st Battalion of the 306 Brigade, where was the logistical base? Was it in the school in Mehurici or was it somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: There are also a few things I'd like to clarify in response to this question. The 1st Battalion of the 306th Brigade was called in that way according to the establishment rules. But in fact, in terms of establishment, it represented one company and it had some attached battalion units. And these were our reserve forces in the case of an attack. Or if there were any problems at the lines, these were the forces we would use to resupply the line. So it wasn't a full battalion. And since it was a sort of manoeuvre unit - it was supposed to be a manoeuvre unit - the equipment that they had was on the whole kept at the command post in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And the command post in Mehurici, was this the Mehurici school? Please say just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, in 1993 how many people were working there at the logistical post in the school in 306, dealing with logistics?

utterances.speaker: MUNIR KARIC
utterances.text: One department at the most -- one squad at the most.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about the presence of the logistical treatment of units in the 306 Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much more time do you need, since it's a quarter to 2.00? Because we withdrew as a result of the objection. But how much more time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I could continue tomorrow, Your Honours, with this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But how much time, how many minutes do you need for this witness now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: In this moment? In general?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I note that the examination-in-chief took one hour and 20 minutes by the Defence. The Prosecution would have questions for this amount of time as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It would be best to adjourn now and continue tomorrow. Sir, you will have to return tomorrow morning since we cannot continue; for technical reasons this is not possible. The courtroom is not available, the interpreters are not available. So please return to the hearing that will start tomorrow at 9.00. I will ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am addressing the Defence now. According to the schedule you have provided us with, this witness should have been examined by the end of today. He'll continue on Wednesday, though. Two witnesses were scheduled for Wednesday. One might be examined on Friday. On Friday there will be another witness. For the two days that remain, Wednesday and Thursday, we have three witnesses. Will you be able to finish with the three witnesses in two days' time?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have already said that on the list we have provided you with there was a mistake because the third witness, Jusic Sejad, was added to it and we heard this witness two days ago. So in fact we have two other witnesses in addition to this one. And I think that we will be able to examine both witnesses, finish the examination of both witnesses by Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We will now adjourn and I will see you all at the hearing at 9.00 tomorrow. We will be continuing with the cross-examination then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
